newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban authorities say Che's legacy still alive.
newsitem.headline: Cuban authorities say Che's legacy still alive.

text.p: Cuban authorities paid tribute to revolutionary hero Ernesto "Che" Guevara on Friday as they awaited confirmation that his remains have been discovered in Bolivia, where he was captured and shot 30 years ago.
"For many generations of Cubans he has a very special meaning," Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina told reporters.
Robaina said Guevara was a living example to younger Cubans who were just children or had not yet been born when he died seeking to spread revolution in Latin America.
To this day, Cuban child "pioneers" vow to be like Che and a giant image of the bearded revolutionary overlooks Havana's Revolution Square.

The Argentine-born doctor, Fidel Castro's right-hand man in the Sierra Maestra armed struggle that led to Cuba's 1959 revolution, was an icon for a generation of leftists around the world and is one of the most revered of Cuba's heroes.

Cuban and Argentine forensic experts examining the remains of what are believed to be seven guerrillas killed in 1967 during a failed uprising in Bolivia said on Thursday they were close to confirming identification of Guevara's remains.
The skeleton known as "E-2" was exhumed last Saturday from a common grave near Vallegrande, a Bolivian town 480 miles (770 km) from La Paz, along with six other sets of bones.
If Guevara's remains are identified, Bolivia has said it will return the remains to his family living in Cuba. The event is expected to bring an outpouring of tributes in Cuba.
Guevara's closest surviving family are his widow Aleida March and four children, Aleyda, Camilo, Celia and Ernesto.
A Cuban Foreign Ministry spokesman said the Cuban Armed Forces would organise a solemn reception of Guevara's remains.
Cuban officials said Guevara's legacy was still relevant in Cuba, even if much had changed on the island since Guevara left to fight in Africa and then Bolivia in the mid-1960s.

"There is sadness because we receive him dead and always would have wanted to receive him alive," said Guillermo Garcia Frias, a former comrade of Guevara's in the guerrilla war in Cuba. Guevara's memory was, he said, "the flag that our youth has to continue the defence of this revolution."

Castro has vowed to stick to one-party socialism despite the crippling blow of the collapse of the Soviet Union and has cautiously liberalised Cuba's economy, eroding socialist orthodoxy by introducing some forms of capitalism.
Some officials said that, despite his tough image and radical plans to forge a "New Man" under socialism, Guevara would have supported changes in Cuba over the past five years.
"I see Che always defending what we are defending...the socialism that we are building," said Robaina.
